tasks.name: Rewire and traverse linked structures safely
Use stack and queue order semantics
Use priority queues for repeated best-item selection

concepts.name: Linked-node rewiring
concepts.description: Manipulate a linked sequence by changing references while preserving access to the remaining chain.

concepts.name: Sentinel / dummy node
concepts.description: Use a non-data node to give head/interior insertion or deletion the same pointer-update shape.

concepts.name: Linked-list reversal state
concepts.description: Reverse a singly linked chain while preserving the unprocessed suffix using previous, current, and next references.

concepts.name: Stack LIFO state
concepts.description: Use last-in-first-out state when the newest unresolved item must be handled before older ones, especially for nested structure.

concepts.name: Queue FIFO state
concepts.description: Use first-in-first-out state when processing order should match arrival order.

concepts.name: Monotonic stack
concepts.description: Maintain only unresolved candidates in monotonic order so each new item can resolve dominated prior candidates once.

concepts.name: Heap priority invariant
concepts.description: Maintain a partial order where the root is always the next minimum or maximum priority item while insertion and removal restore the heap invariant.

concepts.name: Bounded heap for top K
concepts.description: Keep only the best K items seen so far by storing the current cutoff at the heap root.

concepts.name: Heap-based K-way merge
concepts.description: Merge multiple sorted streams by keeping only each stream's current frontier item in a priority queue.

questions.prompt: In a singly linked list, `prev.next` is the node `victim`, and `victim.next` is its successor. You already know `prev`. Which update removes `victim` while keeping the remaining chain reachable?
questions.explanation: Set `prev.next` to `victim.next`. That bypasses victim while preserving the reference to the successor.
hints: The predecessor should point where the removed node used to point.

error_codes.description: The selected update does not preserve the remaining linked chain correctly.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 2 notes: Linked List Sequence
MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Recitation 2: Linked List Sequence

choice_feedback.bridge: Correct: the predecessor now points directly to the successor.
choice_feedback.nullprev: Setting the predecessor's next to None discards the entire remaining suffix.
choice_feedback.self: Pointing victim to itself creates a self-cycle and does not reconnect the list.
choice_feedback.head: Changing head is only required when the logical head itself changes.

questions.explanation: You must save `cur.next` before overwriting it. If `cur.next = prev` happens first, the original forward link is lost unless it was already saved elsewhere.
hints: Ask when the only reference to the rest of the list disappears.

error_codes.description: The update that can lose the unprocessed suffix was not identified.
A valid reversal-state update was incorrectly flagged.

questions.prompt: Order the core updates for one iteration of iterative singly linked-list reversal.
questions.explanation: Save the next node, reverse the current link, advance prev to current, then advance current to the saved next node.
hints: Preserve the only forward link before changing it.

error_codes.description: The reversal updates are out of order.

questions.prompt: You must remove every matching node from a singly linked list, including possibly the first node. Why can a dummy head simplify the loop?
questions.explanation: The dummy gives the logical head a predecessor, so every removal can use `prev.next = cur.next`. The real head is recovered from `dummy.next` afterward.
hints: The awkward case is deleting the first real node.

error_codes.description: The selected reason does not capture the boundary-case simplification provided by a sentinel.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Recitation 2: Linked List Sequence

choice_feedback.same: Correct: it removes the head special case from the pointer-update shape.
choice_feedback.sort: A sentinel does not sort the list.
choice_feedback.random: A sentinel does not provide random access.
choice_feedback.cycle: A sentinel does not detect cycles by itself.

choices.label: It gives the first real node a predecessor, so head and interior removals use the same update
It keeps the list automatically sorted

questions.prompt: A team proposes a linked list for a workload. Which facts would actually support that choice?
questions.explanation: A linked list is attractive when local insertion/removal operations dominate and the code already has the relevant node references. Frequent random indexed access points toward an array-like representation instead.
hints: Look for operations that avoid shifting or indexed traversal.

error_codes.description: A linked-list-friendly workload property was missed.
An operation favoring indexed array access was selected.

questions.prompt: A producer builds a singly linked batch by PREPENDING each new message, so after arrivals A, B, C the chain is C → B → A. Before sending, the batch must be emitted in original arrival order without copying message payloads. What is the direct transformation?
questions.explanation: Prepending reverses arrival order. Reversing the links once turns C → B → A back into A → B → C without copying payload objects into another sequence.

error_codes.description: The selected operation does not directly restore the prepended batch to arrival order.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 2 notes: Linked List Sequence

choice_feedback.reverse: Correct: one link reversal restores the desired order.
choice_feedback.sort: Sorting requires a key and may not preserve original arrival semantics.
choice_feedback.set: A set discards ordering and possibly duplicates.
choice_feedback.cycle: Cycle detection does not change the list order.

choices.label: Reverse the singly linked chain in place
Convert the messages to a set

questions.prompt: A configuration language allows nested `()`, `[]`, and `{}`. While scanning left to right, which structure naturally tracks unmatched opening delimiters?
questions.explanation: Nested delimiters close in reverse order of opening, so the newest unmatched opener must be checked first. That is LIFO behavior.
hints: The innermost still-open scope closes first.

error_codes.description: The selected structure does not model innermost-first closure.

choice_feedback.stack: Correct: nested scopes close in LIFO order.
choice_feedback.queue: FIFO would compare the closer against the oldest opener, not the innermost one.
choice_feedback.heap: Priority does not model nesting order.
choice_feedback.set: A set cannot represent the order of unmatched openers.

questions.prompt: For the delimiter sequence `([{}])`, order these key stack events.
questions.explanation: Opening delimiters are pushed in encounter order. Closing braces pop the newest compatible opener first, unwinding the nested scopes from inside out.
hints: The `{}` pair resolves before `[]`, which resolves before `()`.

error_codes.description: The nested LIFO trace is out of order.

questions.prompt: A simple dispatcher should process waiting jobs in the exact order they arrived. No job has higher priority than another. Which structure directly models the policy?
questions.explanation: Arrival-order service is FIFO: append new jobs at the back and remove the oldest job from the front.
hints: No priority comparison or nesting is required.

error_codes.description: The selected structure does not preserve simple arrival-order service.

choice_feedback.stack: A stack would favor newest arrivals.
choice_feedback.heap: A heap would introduce a priority order not present in the contract.
choice_feedback.set: A set does not preserve arrival order.

questions.prompt: Match each workload to its dominant removal order.
questions.explanation: Nested/undo contexts are LIFO, arrival-order service is FIFO, and 'best priority next' is a priority-queue workload.
hints: Ask what determines the NEXT item to remove: recency, age, or priority.

error_codes.description: At least one workload was matched to the wrong removal-order semantics.
At least one workload was not classified.

items.label: Undo the most recent editor action
Process ordinary jobs in arrival order

questions.prompt: Why is a deque a better general queue primitive than repeatedly calling `list.pop(0)` in Python?
questions.explanation: Python documents deque appends/pops at either side as approximately O(1), while removing index 0 from a list shifts later elements and costs O(n).
hints: Focus on which end is removed and whether later elements must shift.

error_codes.description: A queue-implementation performance fact was missed.
A property not provided by a deque was selected.

evidence.label: Removing index 0 from a Python list requires moving later elements
A deque keeps all elements automatically sorted
A deque automatically removes the highest-priority element

questions.prompt: For each telemetry reading, find the FIRST later reading with a strictly larger value. Which structure avoids rescanning the suffix for every reading?
questions.explanation: A monotonic stack stores unresolved indices. When a larger reading arrives, it resolves and pops every smaller reading exposed at the top. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once.
hints: You need to remember unresolved earlier items and resolve them when a dominating later value appears.

error_codes.description: The selected structure does not preserve the first-later dominance relationship.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 1: Algorithms and Computation

choice_feedback.mono: Correct: it keeps only unresolved candidates in a useful order.
choice_feedback.queue: FIFO order alone does not identify which prior values the new value dominates.
choice_feedback.heap: A heap loses the sequence-local 'first later' relationship.
choice_feedback.sort: Sorting destroys original later/earlier position semantics.

choices.label: FIFO queue of every prior reading
Heap of readings ordered only by value

questions.prompt: A next-greater algorithm keeps unresolved indices in decreasing value order. Flag the update that can lose an unresolved candidate too early.
questions.explanation: An index should be popped only when the current value actually resolves its next-greater answer. Popping an unresolved index merely because a smaller value arrives would discard a candidate with no answer.
hints: Every pop should have a proof that the popped item's answer is now known.

error_codes.description: The premature pop of an unresolved candidate was not identified.
A valid monotonic-stack update was incorrectly flagged.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 1: Algorithms and Computation

elements.label: Push the current index after resolving smaller stack-top values
Pop a top index when the current value is strictly larger and record its answer
Pop the top index whenever the current value is smaller, even though its next-greater answer is still unknown
Leave unresolved indices on the stack when no larger value has arrived

questions.prompt: An editor needs a structure for 'Undo' so the most recently committed edit is undone first. A separate background uploader must process files in the order they were queued. Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Undo is LIFO because the latest action is reversed first. The uploader is FIFO because the oldest waiting file should be processed first.

error_codes.description: The selected pairing does not match the required LIFO/FIFO semantics.

choice_feedback.correct: Correct: newest edit first, oldest queued upload first.
choice_feedback.bothqueue: Undo would reverse the wrong edit order.
choice_feedback.bothstack: The uploader would favor the newest file rather than arrival order.

questions.prompt: A simulator repeatedly schedules new future events and must always execute the event with the EARLIEST timestamp next. Which structure best matches the workload?
questions.explanation: This is a priority-queue workload: inserts continue over time and the smallest timestamp must be extracted repeatedly. A min-heap keeps that next event at the root.
hints: The next item is chosen by timestamp priority, not arrival order.

error_codes.description: The selected structure does not support repeated earliest-priority extraction as directly.

choice_feedback.heap: Correct: repeated insert + extract-min is the priority-queue interface.
choice_feedback.queue: FIFO can execute a later event before an earlier scheduled one.
choice_feedback.stack: LIFO favors newest insertion, not earliest timestamp.
choice_feedback.set: A plain set does not expose the minimum priority efficiently.

questions.prompt: Which statement is guaranteed by a min-heap invariant?
questions.explanation: Every parent is no greater than its children, which guarantees the minimum item is at the root. The rest of the array is not globally sorted.
hints: A heap gives a partial order, not a full sorted order.

error_codes.description: The selected statement is not guaranteed by the min-heap invariant.

choice_feedback.root: Correct: the root is the global minimum in a min-heap.
choice_feedback.sorted: Heap array order is not a globally sorted sequence.
choice_feedback.siblings: Siblings have no required relative order.
choice_feedback.leaves: Leaves are not required to contain the largest items in sorted order.

choices.label: The root is a minimum item
The entire backing array is sorted ascending
Every left child is smaller than its right sibling
All leaves are larger than every internal node

questions.explanation: Queue chooses oldest arrival, stack chooses newest arrival, and heap/priority queue chooses by authored priority.

error_codes.description: At least one removal policy was matched to the wrong structure.

questions.prompt: You have 20 million `(count, key)` pairs and need only the 100 keys with the largest counts. K=100 is tiny relative to n. Which approach best avoids sorting all n items?
questions.explanation: Keep a min-heap of the current top 100. Its root is the weakest current winner; only an item that beats that cutoff needs to replace it.
hints: You only need 100 winners, not a full ordering of 20 million items.

error_codes.description: The selected approach does not exploit K being much smaller than n.

choice_feedback.bounded: Correct: memory stays O(k) and each accepted replacement costs O(log k).
choice_feedback.sort: Sorting all n items works but computes far more order than the output needs.
choice_feedback.max: A max-heap of all n items still stores all n items.
choice_feedback.queue: FIFO order is unrelated to count ranking.

choices.label: Maintain a size-100 min-heap of the current largest counts
Fully sort all 20 million pairs descending
Insert all 20 million pairs into one max-heap before extracting 100
Keep the last 100 pairs in a FIFO queue

questions.prompt: Eight audit files are each already sorted by timestamp and are too large to load fully into memory. You need one globally timestamp-sorted output stream. Which design best fits?
questions.explanation: Keep one current record from each file in a min-heap keyed by timestamp. Pop the earliest, emit it, and refill only from that file. Memory is proportional to the number of streams rather than total remaining records.

error_codes.description: The selected approach does not preserve full global sort order under the streaming-memory constraint.
